newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Palestinians, Israel seek calm before talks.
newsitem.headline: Palestinians, Israel seek calm before talks.

text.p: The Israeli army said it had set up "no-go" areas with the PLO for Palestinian demonstrators in the Gaza Strip on Friday in a bid to prevent further clashes ahead of U.S.-mediated talks starting on Sunday.

The head of the Palestinian side of a joint liaison committee with the Israeli military in Gaza denied any such zones had been established but said there had been agreement on "coordination" to calm tensions.

In Arab East Jerusalem, Moslem clergy stopped protests after Friday prayers at al-Aqsa mosque where extra Israeli police were deployed to prevent a renewal of Israeli-Palestinian violence that has killed 73 people.
Palestinian police kept the lid on protests in other parts of the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

"On the orders of the chief of the Israeli army's southern command, military commanders toured possible points of friction in the Gaza Strip with their Palestinian police colleagues," an army spokeswoman said.

"To reduce this friction and prevent another escalation of (violence), they agreed on and marked security areas of about 300 metres where Palestinian police will prevent the entry of demonstrators," she said.
But the Palestinian liaison official, Brigadier General Zyad al-Atrash, told Reuters: "This is not true. We didn't reach any such agreement. We agreed only on coordination to calm things down."
The Israeli spokeswoman said no buffer zones had yet to be established in the West Bank.
Under interim deals on Palestinian self-rule, Jewish settlements and Israeli soldiers remain in many parts of the West Bank and Gaza pending a final peace accord.

Relations between the Israeli army and Palestinian police have been tense since some policemen took part in gun battles that erupted after Israel opened an entrance to an archaeological tunnel near Moslem holy places in Arab East Jerusalem.
But PLO officials said President Yasser Arafat had ordered his 30,000-strong police force to keep order ahead of Sunday's talks at the Erez crossing point between Israel and Gaza.
U.S. President Bill Clinton said Secretary of State Warren Christopher would go to the Middle East this weekend.
State Department sources said Christopher would meet separately with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Arafat.
The decision to hold the Israel-PLO talks was the main achievement of an emergency White House summit this week to end the worst violence since a 1993 framework peace deal.
Israelis have called the Washington meeting between Netanyahu and Arafat a success. Palestinians deemed it a flop.
Israel's delayed troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron will top the Erez negotiations.

The State Department sources said in Washington it was unclear whether Christopher would be present at the session, moderated by U.S. peace coordinator Dennis Ross. Netanyahu and Arafat themselves are not scheduled to attend.

More than 3,000 Israeli police were deployed in East Jerusalem ahead of Friday Moslem prayers. Unlike last week police did not storm the mosque complex, Islam's third holiest site, as soon as the first rock flew.
Last week they shot dead three Palestinians there. As the first youth shouted "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) religious officials and Palestinian legislators moved in to halt any demonstrations.
The Islamic fundamentalist Hamas movement had called for "total confrontations" with Israeli forces and settlers after Friday prayers.
But Palestinian areas were largely quiet. Israel has ringed PLO-ruled towns with tanks and prevented Palestinians from travelling in the West Bank and Gaza.
